title: Restitution, the Vulnerable, and a Holy People
summary: The ordinances turn to property: stolen livestock, a burglar killed at night, straying animals, fire, goods held in trust, and borrowed animals, each with its rule of restitution. A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride-price. Then the law shifts to capital offenses against God's order and to his protection of the foreigner, the widow, the orphan, and the poor borrower, closing with reverence for God, offerings of firstfruits and firstborn, and the call to be his holy people.
story: The Book of the Covenant continues. Chapter 21 dealt mainly with persons and injuries; chapter 22 begins with property and ends with the heart of Israel's social ethic. Halfway through, the tone changes. The cases stop being framed as if someone does this and become direct commands, with God speaking for himself: “I will surely hear their cry” (verse 23). The people who cried out under Egyptian oppression and were heard (2:23-25) are now told that God will hear the cry of anyone they oppress. The chapter ends with the purpose behind all of it: “You are to be My holy people” (verse 31).
historical:
Israel's economy was farming and herding. Wealth was counted in flocks, herds, grain, and vineyards, and there were no banks, insurers, or police. Neighbors entrusted animals and goods to one another, borrowed oxen for plowing, and grazed flocks beside each other's fields, so most disputes concerned livestock and crops. The Code of Hammurabi addresses the same situations, including deposits, hired animals, and a lion attacking the fold, but it is harsher: theft could require up to thirtyfold restitution, and a thief who could not pay was put to death. Exodus sets restitution at double, fourfold, or fivefold, and a thief who has nothing is sold into service to make it good, not executed for stealing property.

Interest-bearing loans were routine across the ancient Near East, and rates on loans of grain could be steep. Israel's law forbids charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (verse 25; compare Deuteronomy 23:19-20), turning a loan to the poor into help rather than business. An Israelite letter written in ink on a pottery shard, found at Mesad Hashavyahu on the coast near Yavneh-Yam and dated to the late seventh century BC, records a field worker's plea for the return of his garment, which an overseer had confiscated. It shows the kind of case verses 26-27 had in view.
cultural:
Several laws assume customs a modern reader has to reconstruct. A thief who broke in at night could not be seen or identified and might be armed, so the householder who killed him was not guilty; after sunrise, when the thief could be recognized and caught, killing him became bloodshed (verses 2-3). When no witness could settle a case, the parties came before God (the Hebrew is elohim, which the BSB takes as the judges) and swore an oath, trusting God to punish perjury. A shepherd who brought back the torn carcass proved that a wild animal, not his own theft, caused the loss, an image Amos later borrows for the remnant of Samaria (Amos 3:12).

The law on seduction (verses 16-17) assumes the bride-price (mohar), a payment from the groom to the bride's father that sealed a marriage. A man who slept with an unbetrothed virgin had taken what belonged to a marriage, so he must pay the full bride-price and marry her if her father agreed. The cloak law (verses 26-27) pictures the poorest borrower, whose outer garment was also his blanket. A creditor could hold it by day as a pledge but had to return it by sunset.
literary: The chapter has two halves with different voices. Verses 1-17 are case law in the third person, ordered by degrees of responsibility: theft, damage through negligence, loss while in trust, loss while borrowed or hired. From verse 18 the law turns to short, absolute commands addressed to you, much like the Ten Commandments, and God speaks in the first person. Verse 21 adds a motive clause, “for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt,” which turns memory into ethics and recurs throughout the Torah. Verses 22-24 are built on measure for measure: those who make widows and orphans suffer will see their own wives widowed and their children fatherless. Verse numbers in Hebrew Bibles run one lower here than in English, so English 22:18 is Hebrew 22:17.

outline.t: Stolen livestock and the burglar at night
Grazing and fire in a neighbor's field
Property held in trust, borrowed, or hired
Sorcery, bestiality, and sacrifice to other gods
The foreigner, the widow, the orphan, and the poor
Reverence, offerings, and a holy people

doctrines.note: The property laws aim at restitution, not only punishment. The thief repays the owner, the careless neighbor makes good the damage, and the goal is to repair what was broken between neighbors so that the community can go on living together.

God gives his own character as the reason for these laws: he hears the cry of the afflicted and is gracious (verse 27). His compassion makes him the defender of anyone the powerful might crush, even when the oppressor belongs to his own people.

The chapter ends with the call to be God's holy people (verse 31). Holiness reaches from the altar to the lending table and the dinner plate: honoring God, caring for the poor, and refusing the meat of a mauled animal all belong to it.

words.note: Ger, a foreign resident: someone living among a people not his own, without land or clan to protect him. Israel had been exactly that in Egypt, and the law turns that memory into obligation (verse 21). Abraham called himself a foreigner among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), and the Torah repeatedly groups the ger with the widow and orphan as those God particularly guards.

Neshek, interest on a loan. Israel was forbidden to charge it to a poor fellow Israelite, because a loan to someone in need was meant to lift him, not profit from him. Deuteronomy 23:20 permits interest from a foreigner, a distinction that Jewish and Christian authorities debated at length through the Middle Ages.

Channun, gracious, used in the Old Testament almost always of God. He gives it as the reason for protecting a man whose only cloak has been pledged: he will hear, for he is channun (verse 27). The word returns in God's great self-description in 34:6, where the BSB renders it gracious; this small law shows that character at work.

christ: Jesus stands in the line of this chapter's concern for the poor and the outsider. He tells his followers to lend “expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6:35), and James defines pure religion as caring “for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27), echoing verses 22-24. The command in verse 29 to give God the firstborn sons, who were redeemed rather than sacrificed (13:13), lies behind Luke's account of Mary and Joseph presenting the infant Jesus at the temple, because “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord” (Luke 2:23). The God who says he hears the poor because he is gracious is the God the Gospels show in Jesus, moved with compassion for crowds, lepers, and widows. These links are thematic rather than predictive, but they show one God at work across both Testaments.

hard.q: Should the command not to allow a sorceress to live (verse 18) be applied today?
hard.a: Few verses have done more harm in the church's history. In early modern Europe and colonial America, including the Salem trials of 1692, this verse was cited to justify executing people accused of witchcraft, most of them women and many plainly innocent. Reading it well requires distinctions. The law was given to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, where sorcery was treated as treason against the covenant King, beside sacrifice to other gods (verse 20). Christians of nearly every tradition hold that the civil penalties of Israel's law do not carry over to modern states, though they frame the relationship differently; the older division of the law into moral, ceremonial, and civil parts is one common way. The New Testament still treats sorcery as serious sin (Galatians 5:20), but its remedy is repentance, as when new believers in Ephesus burned their books of magic (Acts 19:19), not execution. The witch trials also broke the law's own safeguards, which required credible witnesses and careful judgment before any sentence of death.

questions: Israel was to treat foreigners well because they had been foreigners in Egypt. What part of your own story should make you more merciful to someone else?
A creditor could take a poor man's cloak but had to return it before night. Where do your rights or claims land hardest on someone with less?
These laws aim at restitution, not only punishment. When you have wronged someone, what would it mean to make it right rather than only to feel sorry?
